mandarin-fish.title: Fang et al. (2024): Artificial diets affect glucose and lipid metabolism, antioxidant capacity, and inflammatory response in the muscle of mandarin fish
mandarin-fish.locator: Abstract; Materials and methods / Animal feeding experiment; Table 1; Results
mandarin-fish.access: Public article HTML inspected; model receives these analyst notes, not the full paper.
mandarin-fish.notes: 480 mandarin fish, initial weight 25.1 +/- 0.1 g, were assigned to 12 tanks (40 per tank; six tanks per diet). Eight weeks comparing a particular artificial diet with live prey. Authors reported altered muscle glucose/lipid metabolism, increased malondialdehyde and pro-inflammatory gene expression with artificial diet. These are physiological endpoints, not direct measurements of subjective welfare. Table 1 includes fish meal, krill powder, squid offal and fish oil, so replacement feed is not animal-free. Do not generalize this formula's outcome to all formulations. Trial is not an adoption or economic study. Effects on prey animals and replacement-feed animals were not quantified.

nile-tilapia.title: Pedrazzani et al. (2020): Tilapia On-Farm Welfare Assessment Protocol for Semi-intensive Production Systems
nile-tilapia.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods; Applications and Conclusions
nile-tilapia.access: Public HTML abstract inspected; supplied notes focus on abstract, not a full methodological audit.
nile-tilapia.notes: Protocol feasibility study in three Brazilian semi-intensive farms, examining 139 tilapia. Indicators cover health, environment, nutrition and behavior. Reported critical points included low dissolved oxygen, fin/skin lesions, prolonged handling air exposure and inhumane slaughter practices. Shows feasibility of identifying welfare concerns, not a randomized estimate of welfare improvement from implementing the protocol. Three farms do not establish national prevalence. Direct source funding disclosures were not audited for this sample.

nile-tilapia.title: Terto et al. (2026): Pre-slaughter transport density and seasonal effects on Nile tilapia: welfare and filet quality outcomes
nile-tilapia.access: Public HTML selected sections inspected; full replication and statistical audit not performed.
nile-tilapia.notes: Compared 375, 425 and 475 kg/m3 transport densities across summer and winter, with trips about 1.5 hours. Authors emphasize seasonal thermal and water-quality conditions over small density changes within this high-density range. They explicitly warn tested densities are not welfare-optimal and acknowledge compromised welfare. Do not recommend these densities or infer density never matters. Plasma glucose was higher in winter; avoid assuming hotter season always means worse results. Exact p-values in abstract and results differ for some endpoints; do not repeat them as settled. This sample does not resolve that reporting discrepancy.
